body: Six minutes have gone by with the engine off. The shopping is in the back and it can wait. A man of forty-six is parked outside his own front door at twenty to seven, phone face down on the passenger seat, nothing playing. Through the window he can see the television on and one of his daughters crossing the room with a plate. He has been doing this two or three evenings a week since about February. At ten to seven he picks up the bags, goes in, and when his wife asks how the day was he says it was fine, and most of it was.

He is not hiding anything. There is no other woman, no secret debt, nothing that would make a story. What those ten minutes are for is rehearsal — arriving at a version of the day that will not require anybody in the house to do anything about it.

The standard diagnosis for this is loneliness and the standard prescription is more connection: a group, a breakfast, somebody to check in on a Wednesday. It is well meant and it misses more often than it lands, because a great many of the men in question are not short of company.

What they are short of is a room in which the true answer is available. It is worth taking the word honest literally, because it is not being used to mean confession, or transparency, or any of the words worn smooth by use. It means one specific sentence, said once, at ordinary volume. That the work has been going badly for a year and he has not told anybody. That the marriage is quieter than anyone outside it knows. That the thing he stopped doing has started again. That since the last of the children left he cannot work out what he is for.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air today. A stretch of numbers near the top of the band is set aside for rooms of this kind. The nearest to this article is HM 396.20, Pure Heart Brothers — assigned, in build, not yet on air, still silent.

Holding a number for that is a strange sort of expense. The audience for a frequency about the unsayable is defined by its unwillingness to turn up, which means it will never look good in a report and cannot be sold to anybody. It is held because the shortage it addresses is not the one being counted. Most men have people to talk to and nowhere to say the actual sentence, and those are different shortages, and only one of them gets discussed.

Why the second one goes unnamed is mostly a matter of grammar. Almost everything addressed to men arrives in the imperative. Step up. Lead. Fight. Be the man your family needs. Whatever their merits, imperatives sort a room instantly into those complying and those not, and a man who is failing at the instruction cannot report the failure inside a room organised around it. The register is the barrier. You cannot say you are on the floor in a space whose entire vocabulary assumes you are standing.

The barrier is practical as well. Most of the settings where a man might say something true are settings he has to return to next week — the same touchline, the same office, the same pew, the same brother-in-law at Christmas. The cost of speaking is not the speaking. It is the eleven months afterwards of being looked at slightly differently by somebody who now knows. That is not cowardice. It is an accurate forecast, and it is the reason the sentence stays in the car.
So the problem is not that men will not talk. It is that the first sentence has nowhere to go, and everything useful comes after the first sentence.

The obvious answer is a group, and a group deserves a fair hearing, because groups work. Plenty of men have got out of something bad in a room with six others and a bad urn of coffee, and nobody should be sniffy about that. But a group has an entry requirement that never appears on the flyer: you have to arrive already able to say it. It is built for men who have crossed the line, and the men who need it most are on the wrong side of it, sitting in a vehicle, working out what they will say when somebody asks. The room assumes the sentence, and the sentence is the whole difficulty.
Nobody says the hardest sentence he owns first.

A man of sixty-one drives a forklift on nights at a distribution shed off the motorway. He has one earbud in, against the rules and universally done, and what is playing is not music but two men talking, and one of them says, without any particular weight on it, that there were about two years when he did not like his own company and told nobody, including his wife, particularly his wife. Then they move on to something else. The man on the forklift does not stop, and does not think anything he would call a thought. Nineteen days later, in a hospital car park with his brother, waiting on news about their mother, he says a shorter version of the same sentence out loud. His brother says yes. That is the entire conversation.

Nothing in that required him to speak first. He was not counselled and he decided nothing. He heard the sentence exist in somebody else’s mouth, which removed the only real obstacle, and the obstacle was never courage. It was precedent.

This is not the room, and it would be dishonest to sell it as one. A frequency cannot answer. It cannot notice he has gone quiet for a fortnight, cannot ring on the Tuesday, cannot sit at a table while somebody works up to something over forty minutes. A recording is not a witness. If a man hears the sentence said a hundred times and never says it to anybody with a pulse, the hundred hearings have changed nothing, and counting them would be a lie.

That inability is exactly why it gets listened to. Anything capable of responding has to be faced, and a man who is not ready to be met will not go near it — he will not click, will not go, will not answer the message, and everyone involved will call that reluctance when it is arithmetic about exposure. Something that cannot respond can be left playing while his hands are busy with something else. The limitation is not a weaker form of help. It is the only form that gets through the door at that stage.

The case is narrow and worth keeping narrow. A broadcast does not make a man honest. What it can do is make the sentence ordinary before he needs it — put it in the air at a normal volume, said by somebody unremarkable, at four in the morning, so that when the moment arrives in a car park he is not inventing the language from scratch. The room still has to be found, and the people in it. But the first sentence is where the whole thing jams, and that part can be helped from a distance.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing, so here is the part that is not.

The band carries four kinds of programming and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of it. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them. The block this article has been circling, where Pure Heart Brothers and Iron Sharpening Iron and The Comeback Room sit, is assigned and in build, not yet on air.

What is on air, and nearer the point than it sounds, is HM 315.20 — Corner Cipher. It is a Christian rap station, and plenty of men over forty will bounce off that description. Push past it for one reason. A cipher is a circle: men take turns, one speaks in the first person while the rest listen without interrupting, and nobody is obliged to resolve what he says into something comfortable before the verse ends. Of every form on this dial it is the one least able to hide. The pronoun is I, the tense is now, and the trouble is usually left standing at the end of the bar. An hour of HM 315.20 is a demonstration that a true thing can be said plainly and the man saying it is still there afterwards.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it nearer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So: not a programme to sign up to, and not a step. Put HM 315.20 on for the ten minutes you are already sitting in the vehicle with the engine off. You do not have to agree with it, or like it, and you certainly do not have to tell anybody you had it on. Just hear somebody say a true thing at ordinary volume without the sky coming in. It will not make you honest. It will make the sentence smaller, and the sentence is what has been stopping you.
